kf1.tip: Swap the sprinting push-off for pulling the toes upwards. Say what happens to the roles of gastrocnemius and tibialis anterior, and name the new movement.
kf1.note: The roles reverse. Pulling the toes upwards is dorsiflexion at the ankle. The tibialis anterior becomes the agonist, contracting to pull the toes up. The gastrocnemius becomes the antagonist, relaxing and lengthening to allow the movement. This happens because muscles can only pull, never push, so the ankle needs one muscle for each direction. If you swapped only one role, or still called the movement plantar flexion, look at the box again.

kf2.tip: Choose a movement from a sport you play. Find a concentric, an eccentric and an isometric contraction in it, and name the muscle working each time.
kf2.note: A strong answer names one real movement and finds all three contractions in it, each with a named muscle. Concentric means the muscle shortens to produce movement. Eccentric means it lengthens under tension to brake or control the movement. Isometric means tension with no joint movement. The squat in the box is the model: quadriceps concentric on the way up, eccentric on the way down, isometric in a pause. A common mistake is to call any slow movement isometric. If the joint moves, it is not isometric.

cs1.tip: Write a 3-mark question on the antagonistic pair at the ankle when jumping, then a first sentence of an answer naming joint, movement, agonist and antagonist.
cs1.note: Your question should ask about the ankle during jumping and need three separate points: the movement, the agonist and the antagonist. A good first sentence reads: "During plantar flexion at the ankle joint, the gastrocnemius acts as the agonist while the tibialis anterior acts as the antagonist." If your sentence named the gastrocnemius alone, or left out the joint or the movement, it makes exactly the error the box warns about.
